correctness.rationale: For n≥3 the primary Gaussian zonoid has horizontal and axial support 1 and minimizing-slope orbit support b∞<1 at s0>0. A proposed sharp ellipsoid E with squared support q satisfies b∞²h_Z²≤q≤h_Z². Haar averaging q over O(n−1)×{±1} preserves both inequalities, and the strict α≠1 branches of source Theorem 5.3 force the averaged shape to be Euclidean. Horizontal lower contact and minimizing-slope upper contact fix its scale to b∞². Pointwise inequalities with identical Haar average force equality on entire compact horizontal and minimizing-slope orbits. This fixes the horizontal block and kills cross block w via 2s0<θ,w>/(1+s0²)=0; the axial coefficient is fixed by group averaging. Hence Q=b∞²I exactly; the proof covers all origin-centered ellipsoids in n≥3, not arbitrary translated pairs.

originality.rationale: The full source Ryabogin–Zvavitch proves the sharp Banach–Mazur distance and existence, with strict invariant-ellipse optimization. A symmetry average merely establishes the existence of a symmetric optimum; it does not by itself force every optimizer to be symmetric. The equality-on-contact-orbits step supplies the missing uniqueness. Grundbacher–Kobos general uniqueness criterion d>√(n−1) cannot cover this zonoid for n≥3 because d≤√2≤√(n−1).
residual_risks: Uniqueness might be implicit in an unexamined equality-case argument or alternate normed-space rigidity literature; no exhaustive novelty claim.
The theorem restricts to origin-centered ellipsoids; affine-translated variants not checked.

value.rationale: Characterizing all extremizers, rather than just the optimal distance and existence, is a natural rigidity problem in convex geometry. The argument closes an equality-case gap left by group averaging and identifies the exact centered distance ellipsoid in every dimension n≥3, making it independently useful even though the distance itself is known.

limitations: No uniqueness is asserted for translated ellipsoid pairs or for arbitrary zonoids.
Uses the strict α≠1 part of a genuine prior source theorem as a premise, not an independently re-proven general distance theorem.
